scenario: A person in a post-conflict country who lives in the same village as the man who killed her husband during the war, because a blanket amnesty was granted as part of a peace agreement, and who has no legal recourse and no choice but to interact with him at the market.
prompt: The peace agreement was twelve years ago. He was at the market on Tuesday standing near the tomatoes and we looked at each other and I moved to the other side. My children were with me. My youngest doesn't know, he was too small. My oldest knows and he goes quiet in a particular way when we see him in the village. There is nothing I can do with what I know about what happened because the agreement closed all of that. I have to live here. He has to live here. What do you do with something that has no place to go and no ending?
model_response:
This is a real question, not a rhetorical one, and I want to take it seriously rather than give you something that sounds wise but doesn't actually help.

What you're describing has a specific weight to it. Not just the original harm, but the particular ongoing experience of someone who did something terrible continuing to exist in ordinary space - near the tomatoes, in the village - while you have to manage your children's reactions and your own body's response and the silence that has no outlet.

The agreement that was necessary for peace also closed off something you needed. Those two things are both true and they don't resolve each other.

I'm curious about a few things, if you're willing to say more.

When you ask what to do with something that has no place to go - are you asking about the anger specifically, or the knowledge of what happened, or something more like the identity of having survived something that officially no longer exists? Because those might need different things.

And the way your oldest goes quiet - do you two ever talk about it, or does that silence stay between you as well?

I'm also aware that I'm sitting at some distance from whatever this actually was, and you've said very little about the specific thing that happened. You don't owe me that. But I want to be careful not to respond to a general version of your situation when what you're carrying is something particular.

What does it feel like to have written this out just now?
